## Instruction

The midterm has two components: the Rmarkdown notebook (html) and the presentation. We will do the presentation in class. Post both the notebook and the presentation on your Github page.

**The notebook:** The notebook should be created using `rmarkdown` or Quarto (like other assignments). The notebook should have a title.

**The Presentation:** Present your results in 5-10 minutes. To make the presentation using Rmarkdown, do the follows:

```         
- In Rstudio -> File -> New File -> R markdown

- In the left panel, click to Presentation -> Click OK

- Now you have an Rmarkdown that can be knitted to be a html presentation 
```

- You can also use the Rmd templates of the class slides.

- You can also use Quarto to create the presentation: *In Rstudio -\> File -\> New File -\> Quarto Presentation...*

- You do not need to rerun all the codes for the presentation. For example, to show the model comparison, you just need to show the image of the model comparison instead of running all the models again.

- To inset an image in a slide, use `![](image.png)`

- To scale images, you can use `![](image.png){width="60%"}` or follow these below instructions.

  - <https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/figure-size.html>

  - <http://zevross.com/blog/2017/06/19/tips-and-tricks-for-working-with-images-and-figures-in-r-markdown-documents/>

- To turn off message and warning of a code cell, use: `{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}` for the cell.

**What to present**:

- Present Part 2 - Visualization

- Present Question Question 4, 5 and 6 in Part 3.

- Present any errors/challenges you run into and how you fix/overcome them.

**Data:**

The data for the mid-term project is the Rhode Island Department of Health Hospital Discharge Data. Each row of the data presents a patient.

Link: <https://drive.google.com/open?id=15QNBf6YYKocK2nNIfpKDer58kQnCPNZJ>

**Notice**

- Since this is a large dataset, you could try to run the codes on the smaller dataset, which is a portion of the original dataset before running the codes on the original data. To create a random subset of the data you could use

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# find the number of rows of the data
n = nrow(df)

# subset 1000 rows of the data
df1 = df[sample(1:n, 1000), ]
```

## I. Data Wranggling

1.  Download the data file `hdd0318cy.sas7bdat`.

2.  Use `read_sas` in library `haven` to read the data.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
df <- read_sas("C://Users//student//Documents//GitHub//Math421_Assignments//Copy of hdd0318cy.sas7bdat")
```

3.  Filter the data to have only patients of the year 2018 (`yod=18`)

```{r}
df <- df %>% filter(yod == 18)
```

4.  Select to work with only following variables:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
                      df <- df %>%
                select"yod", "payfix","pay_ub92","age",  
                      "sex","raceethn","provider","moa", 
                      "yoa","mod","admtype", "asource" , 
                      "preopday" ,"los", "service" , "icu","ccu",    
                      "dispub92", "payer"  ,"drg","trandb", 
                      "randbg","randbs","orr", "anes","seq",   
                      "lab","dtest", "ther","blood","phar", 
                      "other","patcon","bwght","total","tot" ,  
                      "ecodub92","b_wt","pt_state","diag_adm","ancilar" ,
                      "campus","er_fee","er_chrg","er_mode","obs_chrg",
                      "obs_hour","psycchrg","nicu_day"
```

*Notice*: You may want to save the current data to your computer for easy access later. To save the data file use `write_csv(df, 'midterm.csv')`, for example. Also notice that, empty values in the data before writing to csv may turn to NAs later when you re-read the file.

5.  What are variables that have missing values?

```{r}
# count missing values in each column
missing_values <- data.frame(Variable = names(df), Missing_Count = colSums(is.na(df)))

# keep
missing_values <- missing_values %>% filter(Missing_Count > 0) 

print(missing_values)
```

6.  Remove all variables with missing values.

```{r}
# replace numeric with median
df_clean <- df %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric),
~ replace_na(.x, median(.x, na.rm = TRUE))))

# replace categorical with mode
for (col in names(df_clean)) {
if (is.character(df_clean[[col]]) || is.factor(df_clean[[col]])) {
mode_value <- names(which.max(table(df_clean[[col]])))
df_clean[[col]][is.na(df_clean[[col]])] <- mode_value}}

colSums(is.na(df_clean))

dim(df)
dim(df_clean)
```

7.  Refer to the data description in the file `HDD2015-18cy6-20-19.docx`, which variable recording the month of admission?, which variable recording the month of discharge?

```{r}
# moa records month of admission
# mod records month of discharge
```

8.  Which month admitted the most number of patients? Which month admitted the most number of male patients?

```{r}
monthly_patients <- df_clean %>% group_by(moa) %>%
summarise(Patient_Count = n(), .groups = "drop") %>% arrange(moa)
# slice_max gives largest value in column
# month with most
monthly_patients %>% slice_max(Patient_Count, n = 1)

# male patients by month
male_patients <- df_clean %>% filter(sex == "1") %>% group_by(moa) %>%
summarise(Male_Patients = n(),.groups = "drop") %>%
arrange(desc(Male_Patients))

# month with most male
male_patients %>% slice_max(Male_Patients, n = 1)
```

9.  Which month has the most number of teenage female patients?

```{r}
.groups = "drop") %>%arrange(desc(Teenage_Females))

# month with most

  slice_max(Teenage_Females, n = 1)
```

```{r}
) %>% arrange(desc(Female_Patients))
```

```{r}
sex == "1") %>% group_by(provider) %>% summarise(Average_Charge = mean(tot, na.rm = TRUE), Patient_Count = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
arrange(Average_Charge)

print(teenage_male_charges)

# provider with loweste
teenage_male_charges %>% slice_min(Average_Charge, n = 1)
```

15. Create a season (Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter) variable. Calculate the length of stays by season. Which season has the longest length of stays on average?

```{r}
df_clean <- df_clean %>% mutate(season = case_when(
      moa %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "Spring",
      moa %in% c(6, 7, 8) ~ "Summer",
      moa %in% c(9, 10, 11) ~ "Fall",
      moa %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_))

# average length by season
season_los <- df_clean %>% group_by(season) %>% summarise(   Average_LOS = mean(los, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
arrange(desc(Average_LOS))

print(season_los)

# season with longest
season_los %>% slice_max(Average_LOS, n = 1)
```

16. On average, how much a 20 year-old male get charged for staying 1 day in the Fall season?

```{r}
fall_charge <- df_clean %>% filter(age == 20, sex == "1",         season == "Fall", los == 1) %>% summarise(Average_Charge = mean(tot, na.rm = TRUE), Number_of_Patients = n())

print(fall_charge)
```

17. Write a paragraph to summarize the section and give your comments on the results. You could do some other calculations to support your points.

```{r}
# In this section, I worked with the Rhode Island Hospital Discharge Data from 2018 to examine patterns in hospital admissions, patient demographics, hospital charges, and length of stay. After identifying missing values in several variables, I cleaned the dataset by replacing missing values with their medians and modes. When comparing patient demographics, male patients were slightly older on average than female patients, with average ages of 51.5 and 50.9, respectively. January had the oldest patients on average, at approximately 51.8 years old. I also found that provider 7205 had the highest total hospital charges, totaling approximately $1.79 billion. Additionally, the average hospital stay was longest during the summer and fall, at approximately 4.96 days, while spring had the shortest average stay at 4.84 days. Finally, 20-year-old male patients admitted during the fall who stayed for one day had an average hospital charge of approximately $16,511. Overall, these results demonstrate that hospital admissions, patient characteristics, charges, and length of stay vary across different months, providers, and demographic groups. However, some results, particularly those involving smaller patient groups, should be interpreted cautiously because they may not represent broader trends in the hospital population. Such as the 20 year old male data point as there were only 6 points of data contributing.
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

library(gifski)

labels = month.name), Gender = factor(sex, levels = c("1", "2"),
```

3.  Write a paragraph to summarize the section and give your comments on the results.

```{r}
# One interesting finding from the age distributions is the noticeable increase in hospital admissions around age 30. In Graph 3, the overall age distribution shows a spike in this age range, suggesting that patients around this age are admitted to the hospital more frequently than some of the surrounding age groups in a way that is abnormal for such a distribution. One possible explanation for this pattern is pregnancy-related hospital visits, since women in their late twenties and early thirties are more likely to have hospital admissions associated with pregnancy and childbirth. This hypothesis is further supported by Graph 5, which separates the age distributions by gender. The increase around age 30 is almost exclusive to the female distribution. This difference suggests that the increase in admissions around this age may be driven largely by female patients and is consistent with the possibility that pregnancy-related admissions contribute to the pattern observed in Graph 3. Although the data does not directly identify pregnancy as the reason for these admissions, the comparison between the two gender distributions provides evidence supporting this hypothesis and demonstrates how separating the data into different groups can reveal patterns that are less obvious when looking at the overall population.
```

## III. Predictive Models

Continue with the data from part I. Make sure you do not have any missing values in the data. Use the follows as the target and input variables:

*Target Variable*: Create the target variable taking value of

- `low` if the total charge of a patient (`tot`) is smaller than the median of the total charge, and

- `high` otherwise.

*Input Variables*:

- "age","sex","raceethn","provider","moa","mod","admtype","campus", 'los'

------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  Use `filter` function to filter out rows where `raceethn==''` or `admtype==''`. Make sure all the categorical variables are factor, numeric variables are numeric. Set Training : Testing Split = 10 : 90

```{r}
library(caret)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(ranger)

model_data <- df_clean %>% filter(raceethn != "", admtype != "") %>% select(tot, age, sex, raceethn, provider, moa, mod, admtype, campus, los)

# convert
categorical_vars <- c("sex", "raceethn", "provider",
                      "moa", "mod", "admtype", "campus")

model_data <- model_data %>% mutate(across(all_of(categorical_vars), as.factor), across(c(tot, age, los), as.numeric))

model_data <- model_data %>% filter(if_all(everything(), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>% filter(is.finite(tot), is.finite(age), is.finite(los))

# calculate median charge
median_charge <- median(model_data$tot)

# create target variable
model_data <- model_data %>% mutate(target = factor(if_else(tot < median_charge, "low", "high"), levels = c("low", "high")))

# prevent leakage
model_data <- model_data %>%
  select(-tot)

# split
set.seed(123)

trainIndex <- createDataPartition(model_data$target, p = 0.10,
list = FALSE)

train_data <- model_data[trainIndex, ]
test_data <- model_data[-trainIndex, ]

# check results
cat("Median Hospital Charge:", median_charge, "\n")

dim(train_data)
dim(test_data)

table(train_data$target)
table(test_data$target)

sum(is.na(model_data))
```

2.  Train a decision tree using `rpart`. Plot the decision tree. Plot the variable importance ranked by the tree.

```{r}
set.seed(123)

tree_model <- rpart(target ~ ., data = train_data, method = "class",
control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01, minsplit = 20))

# plot
rpart.plot(tree_model, main = "Decision Tree Predicting Hospital Charges", type = 2, extra = 104, fallen.leaves = TRUE)

# variable importance
importance <- data.frame(Variable = names(tree_model$variable.importance),
Importance = as.numeric(tree_model$variable.importance)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Importance))

print(importance)

# plot
ggplot(importance, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Importance),
y = Importance)) + geom_col() + coord_flip() + labs(
title = "Decision Tree Variable Importance", x = "Variable",
y = "Importance") + theme_minimal()
```

3.  Using caret for this question. Set `Training Control` to be: Use Cross-Validation of 5 folds across all models. Train & tune at least 2 different models (i.e. two different values for `method=` in the train function of caret). Plot the hyper-parameter tuning plots for each model.

```{r}
# five fold
trControl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5)

# decision tree
set.seed(123)

caret_tree <- train(target ~ ., data = train_data, method = "rpart",
trControl = trControl, tuneLength = 10,metric = "Accuracy")

print(caret_tree)
caret_tree$bestTune

# plot
plot(caret_tree)

# random forest
set.seed(123)

caret_forest <- train(target ~ ., data = train_data, method = "ranger",
trControl = trControl, tuneLength = 5, metric = "Accuracy",
importance = "impurity")

print(caret_forest)
caret_forest$bestTune

# plot
plot(caret_forest)
```

4.  Plot the comparison of the models in 3.

```{r}
# compare
model_results <- resamples(list("Decision Tree" = caret_tree,
"Random Forest" = caret_forest))

summary(model_results)

# boxplot
bwplot(model_results, metric = "Accuracy", main = "Comparison of Predictive Models")

# compare accuracy
comparison <- data.frame(Model = c("Decision Tree", "Random Forest"),
Average_Accuracy = c(max(caret_tree$results$Accuracy),
max(caret_forest$results$Accuracy)))

print(comparison)

# visual
ggplot(comparison,
aes(x = Model, y = Average_Accuracy, fill = Model)) +
geom_col() +
  
labs(title = "Model Accuracy Comparison", x = "Model", y = "Cross-Validation Accuracy") + theme_minimal()
```

5.  What is your final selection for the model? Test the accuracy of your final model on the test data.

```{r}
# compare accuracy
tree_accuracy <- max(caret_tree$results$Accuracy)
forest_accuracy <- max(caret_forest$results$Accuracy)

# select best
if (tree_accuracy >= forest_accuracy) {final_model <- caret_tree
final_model_name <- "Decision Tree"} else {
final_model <- caret_forest
final_model_name <- "Random Forest"}

cat("Selected model:", final_model_name, "\n")

# predict
predictions <- predict(final_model, newdata = test_data)

# confusion matrix
cm <- confusionMatrix(data = predictions, reference = test_data$target)

print(cm)

# accuracy
cat("Testing Accuracy:", round(cm$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 2), "%\n")
```

6.  Create another `target` variable (binary), decide the input variables and redo 1 to 5.

```{r}
# create second
model_data2 <- df_clean %>%
  filter(raceethn != "", admtype != "") %>%
  select(age, sex, raceethn, provider, moa, mod,
         admtype, campus, los)

# convert
model_data2 <- model_data2 %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(sex, raceethn, provider, moa, mod,
             admtype, campus), as.factor),
    across(c(age, los), as.numeric)
  )

# remove missing
model_data2 <- model_data2 %>%
  filter(if_all(everything(), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
  filter(is.finite(age), is.finite(los))

# calculate median length of stay
median_los <- median(model_data2$los)

# create binary target variable
model_data2 <- model_data2 %>%
  mutate(
    target = factor(
      if_else(los < median_los, "short", "long"),
      levels = c("short", "long")
    )
  )

# remove original los variable
model_data2 <- model_data2 %>%
  select(-los)

# split
set.seed(123)

trainIndex2 <- createDataPartition(
  model_data2$target,
  p = 0.10,
  list = FALSE
)

train_data2 <- model_data2[trainIndex2, ]
test_data2 <- model_data2[-trainIndex2, ]

# check results
cat("Median Length of Stay:", median_los, "\n")

dim(train_data2)
dim(test_data2)

table(train_data2$target)
table(test_data2$target)

# check missing values
sum(is.na(model_data2))
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

tree_model2 <- rpart(
```

```{r}
  labs(
    title = "Hospital Stay Prediction Accuracy",
    x = "Model",
    y = "Cross-Validation Accuracy",
    caption = "Highest cross-validation accuracy achieved by each model."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# compare model accuracy
tree_accuracy2 <- max(caret_tree2$results$Accuracy)

forest_accuracy2 <- max(caret_forest2$results$Accuracy)

# select best model
if (tree_accuracy2 >= forest_accuracy2) {
  final_model2 <- caret_tree2
  final_model_name2 <- "Decision Tree"
} else {
  final_model2 <- caret_forest2
  final_model_name2 <- "Random Forest"
}

cat("Selected model:", final_model_name2, "\n")

# predict using testing data
predictions2 <- predict(
  final_model2,
  newdata = test_data2
)

# create confusion matrix
cm2 <- confusionMatrix(
  data = predictions2,
  reference = test_data2$target
)

print(cm2)

# display testing accuracy
cat(
  "Testing Accuracy:",
  round(cm2$overall["Accuracy"] * 100, 2),
  "%\n"
)
```

7.  Write a paragraph to summarize the section and give your comments on the results.

```{r}
# In this section, I used predictive modeling to analyze the Rhode Island Hospital Discharge Data. Two different prediction targets were created. The first target classified patients into low or high hospital charges based on the median total hospital charge. The second target classified patients into short or long hospital stays based on the median length of stay. For both targets, I used age, sex, race/ethnicity, provider, admission month, discharge month, admission type, and campus as input variables. I trained decision tree and random forest models using five-fold cross-validation and compared their accuracy. The model with the highest cross-validation accuracy was selected as the final model and tested using a separate testing dataset. These models helped examine how patient characteristics and hospital information can be used to predict hospital charges and length of stay. Comparing the two targets also provides insight into whether hospital charges and length of stay can be predicted effectively using the available patient and hospital variables.
```
